analysis.one_liner: Bars gas companies from using eminent domain to seize land for LNG export pipelines.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to committee in March 2021 and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have limited the power of natural gas companies to condemn private and state land for pipelines. It would have stopped federal district courts from condemning property in which a state holds any interest, and it would have barred companies from using eminent domain at all for pipelines built mainly to ship liquefied natural gas to foreign buyers. The bill never moved after its referral to the Senate Commerce Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers, ranchers, homeowners, and state governments whose land sits in the path of proposed natural gas pipelines. Under current law, a company with a federal certificate can condemn the land it needs for a route and compensate the owner; this bill would have removed that power for export-oriented pipelines and taken state-owned land entirely off the table for federal condemnation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Landowners in pipeline routes and states

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits United States district courts from having jurisdiction to condemn property in which a state owns any interest, protecting state lands, parks, and holdings from pipeline takings.

Bars any holder of a federal pipeline certificate from exercising eminent domain when the project is to be constructed substantially to transport natural gas to an LNG terminal or other export channels.

analysis.who_pays: Natural gas pipeline companies and LNG exporters, who would lose the condemnation power they currently rely on to assemble pipeline routes across private and state land, and could face higher land-acquisition costs or abandoned export routes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gas pipeline companies and LNG exporters

drawbacks.text: Export pipelines can also relieve domestic natural gas oversupply and support construction jobs, so blocking condemnation authority for export projects could raise project costs, delay projects, or shift routes onto landowners who refuse to sell voluntarily.
The bill leaves ordinary condemnation with compensation in place for non-export pipelines, so landowners on domestic-project routes would get no new protection from this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the landowners targeted — people facing condemnation of a farm, a homestead, or state land so a private company can ship gas overseas — the protection is real and direct. The cost falls on pipeline developers and exporters, and the narrow scope (export projects only) keeps the effect contained. The main weakness is that it leaves most takings for domestic pipelines untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2021 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on March 10, 2021, with Senator Wyden as the only cosponsor.

The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill was not reintroduced in that session, leaving the eminent domain provisions of the Natural Gas Act unchanged.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Natural gas pipeline companies and LNG exporters came out ahead: they kept the full eminent domain power they use to assemble pipeline routes, and landowners along export-pipeline routes got no new protection.

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip eminent domain power from export-oriented gas pipelines and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. Senator (OR); the bill's only cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only additional Senate supporter it attracted.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; took no action on it
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 10, 2021, and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no roll-call split exists; both sponsors were Oregon Democrats and no Republican cosponsor signed on, but the record does not show active opposition either.

industries.note: The bill would have removed their court-backed power to condemn private and state land for export pipelines. Companies profit by building those routes; landowners along them currently bear the taking, compensated at set amounts, so the industry's interest ran against the landowners the bill protected.

The bill specifically targeted pipelines built substantially to feed LNG terminals and other export channels. Losing condemnation authority would have made assembling export routes harder and more expensive.
